findings.where: First screen (hero), desktop and phone; and the style tile as a whole
findings.fault: Mark himself is not on the first screen. There is no portrait and no slot labelled as a stand-in for one. The only picture is the logo mark, drawn very large, and the one line under the name talks about him in the third person ('from a former Lead Lawyer…'). The tile also never shows how a photograph or a video would sit in this world. Its rules are three flat colours with hard edges and no blending, so a reader cannot tell whether Mark's portrait, his project photos or a welcome video belong in this look at all.
findings.who_objects: Mark. His brief asks that he be seen and heard (client value 3), says video is welcome (value 8) and asks for fresh images (§6). Development-bank staff would object too: first-visit trust item 1 expects a real person's face from a solo advisor before they write.

findings.where: The whole direction's tone, most of all the hero: grey stone ground, a monumental mark, the name in carved Roman capitals with interpuncts, all-caps headings throughout
findings.fault: The first impression is a monument or a memorial plaque: a name cut in stone over arches, in a cold grey with no warmth. It does not read as an approachable living advisor. A name inscribed this way, centred under a big emblem, reads like a public-building dedication or an epitaph, not a person you would email.
findings.who_objects: Mark. Client value 1 asks for a personal, approachable advisor, and §5 rejects the reserved, institutional voice. A first-time visitor from a development bank would also get a formal, distant impression where the brief wants one of welcome.

findings.where: Hero headline: 'MARK · M · MOSELEY' over 'INFRASTRUCTURE · ADVISOR'
findings.fault: Both lines are set at the same size, and the job title is the longer line, so it runs much wider and outweighs the name. When you squint, 'INFRASTRUCTURE · ADVISOR' is the line that wins. The page asserts a role category before the person.
findings.who_objects: Mark, whose brief says the individual is the brand (value 1, §5). A visitor scanning the hero takes away a generic job title more than a named advisor.

findings.where: Hero line under the headline (first screen, desktop and phone)
findings.fault: The 5-second test half-passes. The line says what Mark does and gives his credential, but not who the advice is for (development banks and agencies, governments) or where he works. A visitor has to guess whether he serves their kind of body or region.
findings.who_objects: Staff at multilateral development banks, the stated audience (§1). First-visit trust item 2 (what, for whom, where) and item 6 (regions of work) expect them to see themselves on the first screen.

findings.where: Hero, the WRITE TO MARK button; the nav's CONTACT
findings.fault: The one way to get in touch is a label over a mailto link. Mark's email address is never visible on the page, so a visitor cannot see it or copy it.
findings.who_objects: A bank staffer on a locked-down work machine or using webmail, where mailto opens nothing useful and they want to paste the address. First-visit trust item 7 asks for the address in full as its own link text.

findings.where: First screen at desktop: the minium palette swatches showing at the fold under the button; the Texture section's painted red 'M'
findings.fault: The direction reserves minium for the one action, but the next things that catch the eye in red are decoration. On desktop the two red swatch tops show at the bottom of the first screen, right under the button. In the texture, a painted red capital sits in the stone as its loudest mark. On a page with this ground, the red letter would compete with the button for the eye.
findings.who_objects: A first-time visitor, whose eye is pulled to red blocks and a red letter that do nothing. The direction's own 'one accent, and it flows to the action' promise is weakened by them.
